items.q: We've already tried a lot. What's different here?
items.a:
With us, 20 to 40% of the people who attend the masterclass go on to join the training. That comes down to preparation. We put a lot of work into it, because the impact only starts once people take part.

We agree the times with managers in advance, so the training fits into the working week. Your people get to know the programme first, live or in their own time. And we provide the texts, so the invitation comes from your own organisation.

items.q: Doesn't this put the problem on the employee?
items.a: No. You tackle the workload itself through policy: tasks, planning, extra hands in busy weeks. That's still needed. This training comes alongside it. It gives people practical tools for the moments when it still peaks, because those moments won't go away.

items.q: Does everyone have to take part?
items.a:
No, taking part is voluntary. Your people get to know the programme first, live in a masterclass or in their own time. Then everyone decides for themselves.

Our advice: have the invitation come from someone in your own management, saying why you're doing this. People join when they can tell their manager is behind it.

items.q: Is this only for people with stress complaints?
items.a: No, it's for everyone. People who think they're doing fine often notice during the training how much tension they've been carrying without realising. It isn't help for people who are already off sick. It's training to stop it getting that far.

items.q: How does this fit into a full working week?
items.a:
The programme takes one hour a week for six weeks, plus fifteen minutes of practice a day. We fix the times in advance with your managers. And we don't start in the busiest period of your year.

Online and on site both work, and you can choose per group. Research shows online sessions work just as well as in-person ones.

items.q: What about privacy?
items.a:
Every participant gets their own impact report. Individual answers never go to the employer. You only see the results for the group as a whole.

We sign a data processing agreement with you, and the data is stored on servers in Europe.

items.q: How do we pay for this?
items.a: You pay per participant. You get a quote in advance, so you can reserve the budget.

items.q: Can we start small?
items.a: Yes. Start with one school, department or team where the pressure is high and management is on board. If it works, you roll it out further, with the results of the first group to show.

items.q: How do you make sure the learning environment is safe and comfortable?
items.a: The training has weekly group workshops with up to 15 participants. People practise in a safe and comfortable way by responding to concrete questions, without having to share personal stories. So everyone feels at ease and can fully practise with attention.

items.q: 15 minutes of practice a day, how does that work?
items.a: Participants get a workbook at the start with a piece of theory and short exercises for each week. They also receive audio recordings of the exercises. Some exercises can be done during daily routines like brushing your teeth, showering or doing the dishes. So it doesn't cost any extra time. Other exercises take about 12 minutes. For those, you need a quiet spot.

items.q: What are the exercises?
items.a: All exercises are aimed at training attention. The goal is for participants to work and live with more focus and awareness. That's why the exercises are directly applicable in daily life, for example while brushing teeth, eating or walking. Each week also includes a 12-minute exercise.

items.q: What is the foundation of Innerleaps?
items.a: Innerleaps' awareness trainings build on evidence-based programmes such as MBSR, MBCT and WorkplaceMT. The foundation rests on 12 scientific studies, including multiple meta-analyses and randomized controlled trials. The evidence is strong enough that the U.S. military has incorporated attention training into its official doctrine (U.S. Army Field Manual 7-22), and organisations like Google, Apple, Microsoft, Nestlé and Unilever have implemented similar programmes.

items.q: What does an Innerleaps programme deliver for our employees?
items.a:
Research into this kind of training finds less stress, fewer burnout symptoms, more resilience and better sleep. Take stress: compare someone who did the training with someone who didn't, and in 65 to 72% of cases the trained person has less stress.

The risk of long-term absence drops by 70% (from 54.4% to 16.4%). And the drop in stress lasts: studies that checked back three months to a year later still found measurably less stress.

items.q: What is sustainable employability?
items.a: Sustainable employability means employees can keep working in a healthy, motivated and productive way throughout their career. In practice it usually breaks down at the same point: long-term work stress. A quarter of all absenteeism in the Netherlands is stress related. Innerleaps tackles that cause. Employees learn to spot and regulate tension early, so dropout is prevented rather than repaired.

items.q: How do you reduce absenteeism without it staying at symptom relief?
items.a: Reducing absenteeism only works structurally if you step in before people drop out. A quarter of all absenteeism in the Netherlands is stress related. Our training teaches employees to recognise stress signals early, so absenteeism does not just fall but stays low.

items.q: How quickly do we see results?
items.a: Participants notice a difference after the first workshops, and that effect builds up over the six weeks. Straight after the 6-week training, 70% report experiencing less stress. It also lasts: research shows stress stays lower for months after the training.

weeks.title: What you'll <0>actually do</0>
intro: In the workshops you learn new exercises and tools. You practise with them for about 15 minutes a day: partly in your free time, and partly while you're simply doing other things, like brushing your teeth or the laundry.

items.title: Breaking through autopilot
items.text: Where are your thoughts while you brush your teeth? Probably already in your first meeting or your to-do list. Learn to notice when your thoughts wander off and bring your attention back to what you are doing right now. You train your control centre by consciously paying attention to your current activity, again and again.

items.title: Recognising early warning signals
items.text: Train your warning system so you notice tense shoulders, a tight jaw or shallow breathing before tension takes over. You take back control because your sensors get sharper.

items.title: Working with pressure and stress
items.text: Under pressure your working memory often goes haywire. This week you learn a short 3-minute exercise that quickly brings calm and clarity back to your head. You also discover how to plan smart breaks, so you stay sharp throughout the day.

items.title: Mental clarity
items.text: Not every thought is a fact. You learn to recognise the difference between productive thinking and rumination. You also learn to observe your thoughts instead of getting carried away by them. The result: more peace of mind and less worrying.

items.title: Better collaboration through conscious listening
items.text: Under pressure you often start formulating your reply while the other person is still talking. Learn to truly listen, take perspective and respond from understanding instead of reflex.
items.note: Working in education, healthcare or government? Then week 5 is about going easier on yourself when things get busy.

items.title: Lasting integration in your life
items.text: Recognise your thought patterns and make the techniques you learned a lasting part of your daily routine. Build your own toolbox for every situation.

mail.subject: Something for us?
mail.body:
Hi,

As you know, our organisation never stands still. Workload can pile up, and it isn't always easy to focus on your work. I came across Innerleaps ({{link}}). With their attention training they help teams with stress management and focus. It all looks good. They also offer a free masterclass so we can experience the method. Might be good for our next team or company get-together. What do you think?

items.q: Is this woolly?
items.a: No, it's actually very practical. You learn short exercises you can use at work straight away, and you don't have to believe in anything.

items.q: Do I have to talk about myself in the group?
items.a: No. The trainer asks questions and you can respond. What you share is up to you.

items.q: Does my employer see how I'm doing?
items.a: No. If we measure the effect, your employer only sees the results for the whole group.

items.q: How much time does it really take?
items.a: 1 hour a week for the live session, and about 15 minutes of practice, 5 days a week. Some of it you do during things you already do, like making coffee.

items.q: I tried an app and stopped. Why would this be different?
items.a: Almost everyone stops using an app. After a month, about 4 in 100 still use it. Here you practise for 6 weeks with a fixed group and a trainer, and you learn to practise when you feel tension. That's what turns it into a habit.

items.q: What if I miss a week?
items.a: Call or email the trainer and you'll hear what you missed. Everything is in the workbook too. Try not to miss more than 1 session.

items.q: Is it online?
items.a: Usually, yes. No travel time, and you can join from home or the office. On location is possible too.

items.q: How do I get it paid for?
items.a: Ask your manager or HR. Many companies pay from the learning budget. Send them this page, or request a free masterclass together.

items.q: What is it based on?
items.a: Innerleaps' awareness trainings build on evidence-based programmes such as MBSR, MBCT and WorkplaceMT. The foundation rests on 12 scientific studies, including multiple meta-analyses and randomized controlled trials. The evidence is strong enough that the U.S. military has incorporated attention training into its official doctrine (U.S. Army Field Manual 7-22), and organisations like Google, Apple, Microsoft, Nestlé and Unilever have implemented similar programmes.

items.title: The pace is high
items.text: Big ambitions, tight targets and a culture where performing is the norm. After every goal comes the next one, and there's rarely a moment to catch your breath.

items.title: Keeping all the balls in the air
items.text: At work, projects and deadlines run into each other. At home, family and private life need attention too. Your people have little time left to let off steam.

items.title: Lots of distraction, little oversight
items.text: Chat, phones or quickly putting a wash on: there's always something interrupting the work. And with your team working from home some or all of the time, you have little control over how the work gets done.

items.title: Get more done in the same time
bullets: Your team stays on a task longer and gets distracted less.
Fewer mistakes, even when it's busy.

items.title: Owning their own optimal pace
bullets: They know the pace at which they get the most done, and they hold it.
They feel their limit coming and don't go past it.

items.title: A connected and satisfied team
bullets: Six weeks of practising together, in small groups.
Colleagues really get to know each other and become more satisfied with their work.

items.a:
Yes. The training is live and online: one group session of an hour a week, which everyone joins from wherever they work, across countries too. Research shows online sessions work just as well as in-person ones. We pick a time that works for the whole group. On-site is possible too.

Something clients mention themselves: colleagues get to know each other better in the group, even if they rarely meet.

items.q: Can the training be in English?

Our advice: have someone from leadership open the masterclass and say why you're doing this. People join when they can tell their leader is behind it.

items.q: Is this only for people under a lot of pressure?
items.a: No. Think of it as maintenance, like taking your car in for a service before anything breaks. It's meant for the people who work hardest and care most. It isn't help for people who can't cope. It's training for people who want to stay sharp.

items.a: Innerleaps' awareness trainings build on evidence-based programmes such as MBSR, MBCT and WorkplaceMT. The foundation rests on 12 scientific studies, including multiple meta-analyses and randomized controlled trials. The evidence is strong enough that the U.S. military has incorporated attention training into its official doctrine (U.S. Army Field Manual 7-22), and organisations like Google, Apple, Microsoft, Nestlé and Unilever have implemented similar programmes.

items.q: What does an Innerleaps programme deliver for our employees?
items.a:
Research into this kind of training finds less stress, fewer burnout symptoms, more resilience and better sleep. Take stress: compare someone who did the training with someone who didn't, and in 65 to 72% of cases the trained person has less stress.

Productivity goes up too. The effect is smaller, but it is the result the studies agree on most.

The risk of long-term absence drops by 70% (from 54.4% to 16.4%). And the drop in stress lasts: studies that checked back three months to a year later still found measurably less stress.

items.q: How does Innerleaps improve employee performance?
items.a:
Innerleaps improves performance by optimizing working memory, the mental "workspace" where thinking, deciding and acting take place. This happens through three mechanisms:

First, relevant information is selected faster and irrelevant information is suppressed more effectively. Focus increases, distraction decreases. Research shows 25% fewer errors on attention tasks (Jha et al., 2021).

Second, stress and pressure normally occupy a large share of working memory. When that pressure decreases, capacity is freed up for the task itself.

Third, working memory becomes more efficient: better results with less neural effort (Bailey et al., 2020). Employees perform sharper and have energy left at the end of the day.
